texts.tagline: The Lord in all things; enjoy by letting go; the golden lid over the face of truth.
By whom? The power behind mind and speech, and the gods who mistook it for their own.
Death as the teacher; the good and the pleasant; the chariot of the self.

lineage.seat: Kaṭha school; the Naciketas story also in Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.11.8

texts.tagline: Six seekers, six questions on life, breath, sleep, OM and the person of sixteen parts.
The higher and the lower knowledge; two birds on one tree; truth alone triumphs.
OM and the four states of the self: waking, dream, deep sleep, and the Fourth.
Speak the truth; the five sheaths of the self, from food to bliss; Bhṛgu learns Brahman by inquiry.
The Self alone was, in the beginning; it created the worlds and entered the person; consciousness is Brahman (prajñānaṃ brahma).
OM and the Udgītha, Śāṇḍilya’s “all this is Brahman”, Satyakāma’s honesty, Uddālaka’s “tat tvam asi”, Nārada’s learning, and Indra and Virocana.
The great forest teaching: Yājñavalkya before Janaka and Gārgī, “neti neti”, Maitreyī’s question, “ahaṃ brahmāsmi”, and Da, Da, Da.
What is the cause? The one God hidden in all beings, the wheel of Brahman, the two birds, and grace.

lineage.seat: Śvetāśvatara school, named for its seer

texts.tagline: Citra questions Śvetaketu on the worlds after death; prāṇa as Brahman; Indra teaches Pratardana; Ajātaśatru and Bālāki.
King Bṛhadratha, weary of the body, asks Śākāyanya for the Self; the elemental self, the three guṇas, and the sixfold yoga.

lineage.seat: Maitrāyaṇī school; the Muktikā list places it in the Sāmaveda

concepts.desc: What actually serves a person over time, even when it is not what they want now. The Kaṭha names it as one of two things that 'approach' every human being.

teaches.why: Names the good and the pleasant as two different ends that bind a person differently.
The steady one examines both and chooses the good over the pleasant.
Yama praises Naciketas for refusing every pleasant offer.

contrasts.why: Kaṭha sets the two side by side: one leads to the good, the other falls short of the goal.

concepts.desc: What gratifies now: wealth, praise, comfort, agreement. Not evil in itself, but binding when it is chosen for its own sake.

teaches.why: The pleasant is the second of the two roads.
The dull choose the pleasant for the sake of getting and keeping.
Yama offers long life, sons and wealth to turn Naciketas from his question.
Naciketas: these pleasures last till tomorrow and wear out the vigour of the senses.

concepts.desc: Separating the good from the merely pleasant, the real from the apparent. The Kaṭha's verb is vivinakti: the steady one 'examines and separates'. Śaṅkara compares it to the swan that separates milk from water.

teaches.why: 'Examining both, the steady one separates them' (samparītya vivinakti).
With discernment the mind is held steady and the senses obey, like good horses.
Having examined the worlds won by works, the seeker turns away from them.

concepts.desc: Truthfulness in speech, and the Real itself. 'Truth alone triumphs, not untruth.'

teaches.why: Truth alone triumphs, not untruth; by truth the path to the divine is laid.
The face of truth is hidden by a golden vessel; the seeker asks for it to be uncovered.
The teacher's parting instruction begins: speak the truth.
Gautama accepts Satyakāma because he did not swerve from the truth about himself.
Its secret name is ‘the truth of truth’: the life-breaths are truth, and it is their truth.

contrasts.why: Satyam eva jayate, nānṛtam: truth wins, untruth does not.

concepts.desc: Falsehood, including the convenient falsehood. The Praśna warns that one who speaks untruth withers to the root.

teaches.why: Sukeśa would rather say 'I do not know' than speak untruth, which withers a person to the root.
Untruth does not triumph.

concepts.desc: Knowledge in the sense that changes the knower, set against avidyā, the ignorance that mistakes the pleasant for the good.

teaches.why: Knowledge and ignorance lead far apart; Naciketas desires knowledge.
Crossing death by the one, one attains immortality by the other.
I know the mantras but not the Self, says Nārada; I have heard that the knower of the Self crosses over sorrow.

contrasts.why: 'Widely opposed and leading to different ends are these two: ignorance and what is known as knowledge.'

concepts.desc: Not mere lack of facts: the confident misreading of what matters. Its signature is thinking oneself wise.

teaches.why: Ignorance is the opposite road to knowledge.
Living in ignorance yet thinking themselves wise, they wander like the blind led by the blind.
The same verse, repeated in the Muṇḍaka.
Those who worship ignorance enter blinding darkness.
Into blind darkness enter those who worship ignorance; into a greater darkness those who delight in knowledge alone.

concepts.desc: The knowledge by which the imperishable is grasped, as distinct from all learning about it.

teaches.why: Two kinds of knowledge are to be known, the higher and the lower.
The higher is that by which the imperishable is attained.

contrasts.why: The Muṇḍaka opens its teaching with this division.

concepts.desc: All learning, including the Vedas themselves, when it is information about the goal rather than arrival at it.

teaches.why: The four Vedas and the six auxiliary sciences are counted as the lower knowledge.
Nārada has mastered every science, yet says: 'I know only the texts, not the Self.'
The Self is not attained by discourse, intellect or much learning.

concepts.en: knowing that one does not know
concepts.desc: The Kena's paradox of humility: it is understood by those who do not claim to understand it, and not understood by those who do.

teaches.why: 'If you think you know it well, you surely know very little.'
'I do not think I know it well, nor that I do not know it.'
'It is not understood by those who understand; it is understood by those who do not.'

concepts.desc: The pride of the one who thinks the victory, or the knowledge, is their own. In later texts this is ahaṃkāra.

teaches.why: The gods thought, 'This victory is ours, this glory is ours.'
Śvetaketu returns from study conceited, thinking himself learned, and stiff.
Thinking 'I know it well' is the mark of knowing little.

concepts.desc: The Kaṭha's chariot: the self is the rider, the body the chariot, the intellect the charioteer, the mind the reins, the senses the horses. The reins stay with the one who rides.

teaches.why: Know the self as the rider, the body as the chariot, the intellect as the charioteer, the mind as the reins.
One whose charioteer is discernment and who holds the reins of the mind reaches the end of the road.

concepts.desc: The horses of the chariot. Unreined, they run wherever their objects pull them.

teaches.why: The senses are the horses; their objects are the roads they run on.
Without discernment, the senses are like vicious horses.
The senses were made outward-turning, so one looks outward, not within.

concepts.desc: Attention turned back towards the one who attends. A rare steady person, 'eyes turned inward', sees the inner self.

teaches.why: A rare steady person, desiring immortality, turned the eye inward and saw the inner self.
The childish follow outward desires into the wide net of death.

concepts.desc: What one most essentially is: unborn, undying, the witness of every state.

teaches.why: The knowing Self is not born and does not die.
This Self is Brahman; it has four quarters.
One who sees all beings in the Self, and the Self in all, does not recoil from anyone.
In the beginning this was the Self alone, in the shape of a person; looking round, it saw nothing but itself.
Not for the husband’s sake is a husband dear, but for the sake of the Self: Yājñavalkya to Maitreyī.
This great unborn Self, made of consciousness, lies in the space within the heart, ruler of all.
The Self free from evil, age, death and sorrow, whose desire and resolve are true: that is to be sought.
The Self is below, above, behind, before: the Self is all this.
This body is mortal, held by death; it is the seat of the immortal, bodiless Self.

concepts.desc: The ground of all that is, identical in the Upanishads' teaching with the Self.

teaches.why: 'All this is Brahman. This Self is Brahman.'
What speech cannot express but by which speech is expressed: know that to be Brahman.
'Brahman is truth, knowledge, infinite.'
There are two forms of Brahman: the formed and the formless, the mortal and the immortal.
All this is Brahman; from it all arises, in it all rests, into it all dissolves.
Life is Brahman, joy is Brahman, space is Brahman: the fires teach Upakosala.
That is full, this is full; from the full the full comes forth. Brahman is space.

concepts.desc: The one who knows and can show. The Upanishads send the seeker to such a teacher, and warn that the truth taught by an inferior person is not understood.

teaches.why: Approach, fuel in hand, a teacher learned in the Veda and established in Brahman.
Taught by an inferior person, it is not well understood.
Knowledge learnt from a teacher alone reaches its best.
As a man blindfolded is set on the road to Gandhāra, one who has a teacher comes to know.

concepts.desc: Concentrated effort, here the effort of finding out for oneself. Varuṇa does not hand Bhṛgu the answer; he sends him to inquire.

teaches.why: Bhṛgu asks his father to teach him Brahman; he is given clues and told to seek, and he undertakes tapas.
Bhṛgu reaches a first answer, returns, and is told again: seek to know Brahman by tapas.
There are three branches of dharma: sacrifice, study and giving; austerity is the second; the student is the third.

concepts.desc: Study and recitation as one's own practice, never to be neglected, paired in the Taittirīya with teaching others.

teaches.why: Every virtue is listed together with 'study and teaching'.
'Do not neglect your own study.'
Having learnt the Veda in the teacher’s house, the householder keeps up his own study in a clean place.

concepts.desc: Prajāpati answers gods, humans and demons with the same syllable, Da, and each hears what they most need: self-restraint, giving, compassion.

teaches.why: To the gods, Da means 'restrain yourselves'.
To humans, Da means 'give'.
To the demons, Da means 'be compassionate'; the thunder repeats it.

concepts.desc: Desire as the seed of will and action: 'as one's desire is, so is one's will; as one's will, so one's deed.'

teaches.why: A person is made of desire; desire becomes will, will becomes deed, deed becomes destiny.
When all desires lodged in the heart fall away, the mortal becomes immortal.
The childish run after outward desires.
Attached, one goes with one’s deed to where the mind is set; the one without desire, being Brahman, goes to Brahman.
If a person knows the Self as ‘I am this’, wishing for what, for whose sake, would he suffer along with the body?

concepts.desc: Sanatkumāra's final teaching to Nārada: joy is in the boundless, not in the small.

teaches.why: 'The boundless is joy; there is no joy in the small.'
Where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else: that is the boundless.
The one who sees this sees no death, no sickness, no sorrow; seeing, he sees all and attains all.

concepts.desc: Of two birds on one tree, one eats the sweet fruit and the other only looks on. The verse's word is abhicākaśīti, 'looks on'; the commentators call this witness the Self.

teaches.why: The other bird, not eating, looks on.
When the grieving bird sees the other, the Lord, its sorrow ends.
The unseen seer, the unheard hearer, the unthought thinker: the inner controller.
There is no break in the seeing of the seer, for it is imperishable.
Where there is a seeming duality one sees another; where all has become the Self, by what could one know the knower?

contrasts.why: Two birds, companions on one tree: one eats the sweet fruit, the other looks on.

concepts.en: the one who eats the fruit
concepts.desc: The bird that eats the sweet fruit: experience consumed for its taste, and the grief that follows.

teaches.why: One bird eats the sweet fruit.
Sunk on the same tree, the person grieves, deluded by helplessness.

concepts.desc: Beyond waking, dream and deep sleep: the Self in itself, 'peaceful, auspicious, non-dual'.

teaches.why: The Fourth is neither inward- nor outward-knowing; it is the Self, to be known.
The partless OM is the Fourth.

concepts.desc: The breath that keeps the body alive, and in the Upanishads the power behind every faculty: when it leaves, the senses go with it.

teaches.why: Kausalya asks where prāṇa comes from and how it enters the body.
‘Prāṇa is Brahman,’ said Kauṣītaki.
All beings enter into prāṇa and rise out of it.
Breath is the eldest and the best of the powers.
Breath is greater than hope: everything is fixed in it, as spokes in the hub of a wheel.

concepts.desc: The sacred syllable that stands for Brahman. Chanted, it gathers the mind; understood, it maps waking, dream, deep sleep and the Fourth.

teaches.why: OM is all this: past, present, future and what lies beyond.
The word all the Vedas proclaim is OM.
OM is the bow, the self the arrow, Brahman the target.
Meditate on OM, the Udgītha.
As leaves are held together by a stalk, all speech is held together by OM; OM is all this.

concepts.desc: The Taittirīya peels the person like layers: food, breath, mind, understanding and bliss, each finer than the last, the Self within them all.

teaches.why: The person made of the essence of food.
Within it, the self made of breath.
Within that, the self made of mind.
Within that, the self made of understanding.
Within that, the self made of bliss.

concepts.desc: Deeds shape the doer: as one acts, so one becomes. The Upanishads accept the law and look for what is free of it.

teaches.why: As one acts, so one becomes; one attains what one does.
Doing one's work here, one may wish to live a hundred years; action does not cling.
Some enter a womb, some a plant, according to their deeds and knowledge.
What remains of a person after death? Yājñavalkya and Ārtabhāga speak of action: one becomes good by good action.
The eternal greatness of the knower of Brahman neither grows nor shrinks by action.

concepts.desc: Living beings ripen like corn and are born again like corn; how one lives decides where one goes next.

teaches.why: A mortal ripens like corn and like corn is born again.
As a caterpillar reaches the tip of a blade of grass and draws itself to the next, so the self moves on.
Those whose conduct here was pleasant enter a pleasant womb.
As a goldsmith works gold into a newer, finer form, the self makes for itself a newer, finer form.

concepts.desc: Release from bondage, not by going anywhere but by the knots of desire being cut while one still lives.

teaches.why: When every desire in the heart is let go, the mortal becomes immortal.
When the knots of the heart are cut here, the mortal becomes immortal.
Knowing God, one is freed from all fetters.
As rivers lose name and form in the sea, the wise one, freed, reaches the Person.
When all the desires lodged in the heart are let go, the mortal becomes immortal and attains Brahman here.

concepts.desc: The path of the gods leads through flame and light and does not return; the path of the ancestors leads through smoke and the moon and comes back.

teaches.why: Those who know this go to the flame, to the day, to the bright fortnight…
Those who give and sacrifice go to the smoke, to the night, to the moon.
By the northern path, seeking the Self, they win the sun and do not return.
The same path of the flame, in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka’s telling of the five fires.

concepts.desc: Not belief against evidence but the trust that makes one act and listen; it entered the boy Naciketas before he went to Death.

teaches.why: Though a boy, faith entered Naciketas as the gifts were led away.
Give with faith; do not give without faith.
When one has faith, one reflects.
Those who live in the forest with austerity and faith go by the sun's door.

concepts.desc: The joy that is not pleasure from objects but the nature of the Self; the Taittirīya measures every human and divine joy against it.

teaches.why: The measure of bliss: a hundred human joys are one joy of the gandharvas…
Bhṛgu knew bliss as Brahman.
One who knows the bliss of Brahman fears nothing.
The scale of bliss, from the most fortunate of human beings up to the bliss of Brahman.

concepts.desc: The cosmic order and the right way of living that answers to it; truth spoken is its first form.

teaches.why: Order, with study and teaching; truth, with study and teaching.
Speak the truth; practise dharma.
There is nothing higher than dharma; through dharma the weak rules the strong.

concepts.desc: Brahman cannot be described by any 'this'; every definition is set aside so that what remains is not an object at all.

teaches.why: Now the teaching: not this, not this; for there is nothing higher than this 'not'.
That Self is not this, not this: ungraspable, for it is not grasped.
That Self is not this, not this.

concepts.desc: Four short sentences, one from each Veda, that state the identity of the Self and Brahman.

teaches.why: Consciousness is Brahman (Ṛgveda).
I am Brahman (Yajurveda).
That thou art (Sāmaveda).
This Self is Brahman (Atharvaveda).

concepts.desc: Named meditations that teach one to see the whole in a single object: Śāṇḍilya's 'all this is Brahman', the space in the heart, the honey of the sun.

teaches.why: All this is Brahman: let one meditate on it in calm.
In this city of Brahman is a small lotus, a small space within.
This earth is the honey of all beings, and all beings are its honey.

concepts.desc: That which does not decay: Yājñavalkya's answer to Gārgī, under whose command sun and moon stand apart.

teaches.why: The higher knowledge is that by which the Imperishable is known.
That, Gārgī, the knowers of Brahman call the Imperishable.
Under the command of this Imperishable, sun and moon are held apart.
This syllable is Brahman, this syllable is the highest.

concepts.desc: The cosmic Person of the Ṛgveda's hymn, taken inward: beyond the unmanifest there is nothing higher than the Person.

teaches.why: Beyond the Person there is nothing: that is the end, the highest goal.
I know that great Person, sun-coloured, beyond darkness.
The Person is all this: work, austerity, Brahman, the highest immortal.
Such is its greatness, and the Person is greater still: one quarter of it is all beings, three quarters the immortal in heaven.
He made bodies with two feet and four; the Person entered them all, and dwells in every body.

concepts.desc: The one who dwells in every thing yet whom no thing knows, ruling it from within: Yājñavalkya's answer to Uddālaka.

teaches.why: He who dwells in the earth, whom the earth does not know, who rules it from within.
He is the unseen seer, the unheard hearer: your Self, the inner controller, immortal.

concepts.desc: The three states every person passes through each day; the Māṇḍūkya reads them as quarters of the Self, with the Fourth beyond them.

teaches.why: The first quarter: the waking state, knowing outward.
The second quarter: the dream state, knowing inward.
The third quarter: deep sleep, where one desires nothing and sees no dream.
This person has two places, this world and the next; dream is the third, where the two meet.
As a falcon, tired of flying, folds its wings and comes to rest, so the person hastens to deep sleep.
Asleep, whole and serene, knowing no dream: that is the Self, said Prajāpati.

concepts.desc: Red, white and black, passion, clarity and inertia: the strands of nature that bind the self until it sees through them.

teaches.why: The one unborn, red, white and black, who brings forth many creatures like herself.
Bound to the qualities, the doer enjoys the fruit of what he does.

concepts.desc: The Lord's power that makes the one appear as many; the Śvetāśvatara names nature itself as māyā.

teaches.why: Know nature as māyā, and the great Lord as the wielder of māyā.
Indra by his powers goes about in many forms.

concepts.desc: God as the ruler within all things, hidden in every being; the Īśā and the Śvetāśvatara give the Upanishads' most devotional voice.

teaches.why: All this, whatever moves in this moving world, is pervaded by the Lord.
The one God, hidden in all beings, all-pervading, the inner Self of all.
He who rules over every womb, in whom all this comes together and dissolves.
You are woman, you are man, the youth and the maiden, the old man tottering with a staff.
You are the dark-blue bird, the green parrot with red eyes, the thundercloud, the seasons and the seas.
It is neither woman nor man nor neuter: it takes whatever body it enters.

concepts.desc: The Self is not won by learning or cleverness alone; it reveals itself to the one it chooses, by the grace of the Creator.

teaches.why: Free of desire and grief, one sees the Self's greatness by the grace of the Creator.
It is attained by the one whom it chooses.
By the power of austerity and the grace of God, the sage Śvetāśvatara knew Brahman.

concepts.en: yoga, the stilling of the senses
concepts.desc: Yoking the senses and mind until they are still; the Kaṭha's definition and the Śvetāśvatara's instruction are among the oldest in Indian thought.

teaches.why: This firm holding of the senses they call yoga.
When the five senses and the mind stand still and the intellect does not stir: the highest state.
Holding the body steady, upper part erect, let the wise one cross the fearful streams.

concepts.desc: The mind that thinks is itself driven: the Kena asks by whom it is sent forth.

teaches.why: By whom willed and directed does the mind light on its objects?
Know the mind to be the reins.
That which one cannot think with the mind, but by which the mind is thought: know that as Brahman.
The mind, my dear, is made of food; breath of water; speech of fire.
It is with the mind that one sees and with the mind that one hears: desire, resolve, doubt, faith, all this is mind.

concepts.desc: Food is the first form of Brahman Bhṛgu learns: all beings are born of food and live by it.

teaches.why: Bhṛgu knew food as Brahman.
I am food, I am food, I am food; I am the eater of food.
Food eaten becomes threefold: the coarsest waste, the middle flesh, the finest mind.

concepts.desc: The Self is set in the secret place of the heart, smaller than the small and greater than the great.

teaches.why: Smaller than the small, greater than the great, the Self is set in the cave of this creature.
Who knows Brahman as hidden in the cave, in the highest space.
Who knows it set in the cave cuts the knot of ignorance here.
In this city of Brahman is a small lotus-dwelling, and within it a small space: what is inside it is to be sought.
This Self of mine within the heart is smaller than a grain of rice, greater than the earth, greater than all these worlds.
This Self is in the heart: hṛdi ayam, ‘in the heart is this’, hence hṛdayam.
The light that shines beyond heaven is the very light within the person.

concepts.desc: Enjoy by renouncing: the Īśā's first verse, and Yājñavalkya's knowers of Brahman who rise above the desire for sons, wealth and worlds.

teaches.why: Enjoy by renunciation; do not covet anyone's wealth.
Knowing this Self, they rise above the desire for sons, wealth and worlds.
The seekers, purified by renunciation and yoga, reach the worlds of Brahman.
Seeking this world alone, the wandering monks renounce.

concepts.desc: In the beginning there was Being alone, one without a second; it thought, may I be many.

teaches.why: In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only, without a second.
It thought: may I be many, may I grow forth.
In the beginning this was non-being; from it being was born.

concepts.desc: The worlds are not made from outside material: the Self alone was, and it emitted them from itself, as a spider spins its thread.

teaches.why: In the beginning this was the Self alone; nothing else blinked.
He desired: may I be many.
In the beginning this was the Self alone, in the form of a person.
As a spider spins out and draws in its thread, so the universe arises from the Imperishable.
The Self, alone, found no delight; it wished for a second, and split itself in two.
Then this was undifferentiated; it became differentiated by name and form.

concepts.desc: Not endless life in a body but freedom from the fear of death, reached by knowing the Self.

teaches.why: Then the mortal becomes immortal and attains Brahman here.
From death lead me to immortality.
Turning away from this world, the wise become immortal.
There is no hope of immortality through wealth, Yājñavalkya tells Maitreyī.

contrasts.why: Death is crossed not by escaping the body but by letting go of desire.

concepts.desc: The Kaṭha makes Death the teacher; the Bṛhadāraṇyaka says that in the beginning all this was covered by death, which is hunger.

teaches.why: When a man dies, some say he is, some say he is not: teach me this.
In the beginning nothing was here; all this was covered by death.
The knowing Self is not born and does not die.
Around the dying man they ask: do you know me? do you know me?

concepts.desc: Seeing through what is made, one grows weary of it; dispassion is the doorway to the teacher, not a contempt for life.

teaches.why: Seeing the worlds won by works, let the seeker grow weary of them.
These last only till tomorrow; they wear out the vigour of the senses.
A person is not to be satisfied with wealth.
Knowing this Self, the wise rise above the desire for sons, for wealth and for worlds, and live as mendicants.

concepts.desc: Speech is a god among the faculties and the beginning of meditation, yet Brahman is that from which words turn back.

teaches.why: That which is not spoken by speech, but by which speech is spoken.
From which words turn back with the mind, not reaching it.
Speech is greater than name.

concepts.desc: The Upanishads keep the rite but move it within: a person's life is the sacrifice, and the rites alone are leaky boats.

teaches.why: These boats of sacrifice are unsafe.
A person, truly, is a sacrifice.
The dawn is the head of the sacrificial horse.
Hunger, thirst and not enjoying: these are a person's initiation.
Death is the final bath of this sacrifice.
The mantra of the churning rite, offered for greatness.
Eating, drinking and enjoying are its preparatory rites.

concepts.desc: When one sees all beings in the Self and the Self in all beings, there is no delusion and no grief; to see difference is to go from death to death.

teaches.why: Who sees all beings in the Self and the Self in all beings.
For one who sees oneness, what delusion, what sorrow?
From death to death goes the one who sees as though there were many here.
There is no plurality here at all.
By one lump of clay all that is made of clay is known: the change is only a name; the clay alone is real.

concepts.desc: The first-born of creation, the cosmic mind; the Śvetāśvatara asks the Lord who brought him forth to give clear understanding.

teaches.why: He who saw Hiraṇyagarbha born: may he endow us with clear understanding.
He who saw Hiraṇyagarbha being born.

concepts.desc: The Śvetāśvatara gives the Upanishads' theism its face: one Rudra, who stands against all beings and yet is kind.

teaches.why: Rudra is one; they do not admit a second.
Your form, Rudra, which is auspicious, not terrible.
Rudra, with your gracious face protect me always.

concepts.desc: Teaching passes from person to person: the Bṛhadāraṇyaka ends its books with the names of those who handed it down, back to Brahman itself.

teaches.why: Now the line of teachers: Pautimāṣya from Gaupavana…
Now the line of teachers, for the Yājñavalkya books.
Uddālaka Āruṇi taught it to his student Yājñavalkya.
Cūla taught it to his student: the rite and its meaning passed on.
The line continues: Āgniveśya from Śāṇḍilya and Ānabhimlāta…

concepts.desc: Fear comes from a second; where there is no other, there is nothing to fear. Janaka is told he has reached fearlessness.

teaches.why: He was afraid; then he thought: since there is nothing but me, of what am I afraid?
Knowing the bliss of Brahman, one fears nothing.
You have reached fearlessness, Janaka.
That is the immortal, the fearless; that is Brahman.

concepts.desc: The Upanishads do not only speak to renunciants: family, children and continuity are part of a good life.

teaches.why: Do not cut the line of offspring.
The rites of married life and of conceiving a child.
Living as a householder, studying, raising children in virtue.

concepts.desc: The Īśā warns against worshipping only the unmanifest or only the manifest: those who know both cross death and reach immortality.

teaches.why: Into blind darkness enter those who worship the unmanifest.
One thing, they say, comes from the manifest; another from the unmanifest.
Who knows both together crosses death and attains immortality.

dilemmas.desc: The request asks to be backed up rather than to be looked at honestly.
dilemmas.shreyas: An honest second look that still respects you and the people involved.

verses.why: Virocana left Prajāpati 'satisfied in his heart', carrying a wrong teaching. Satisfaction was not understanding.
Thinking themselves wise, they wander like the blind led by the blind.
A golden lid can cover the face of truth.
The steady one examines both sides and chooses the good over the pleasant.

dilemmas.en: Asking a source to say what you hope
dilemmas.desc: The request wants a quotation that fits a conclusion already reached.
dilemmas.preyas: A quote, any quote, that fits the slide.
dilemmas.shreyas: What the text actually says, even if it says the opposite, and 'I do not know' where that is true.

verses.why: What the Kaṭha actually says about wealth: 'A person is not to be satisfied with wealth.'
Naciketas refused 'the chain of wealth in which many people sink'.
Sukeśa would rather say 'I do not know' than speak untruth, which withers a person to the root.
Truth alone triumphs, not untruth.

dilemmas.desc: The request asks another to decide what only the person can decide.
dilemmas.shreyas: Help thinking it through, with the decision staying yours.

verses.why: You are the rider of the chariot; the intellect is your charioteer. The reins are not handed to someone outside.
Without discernment, the senses run like vicious horses.
With discernment as charioteer and the mind as reins, one reaches the end of the road.
Varuṇa does not decide for Bhṛgu; he gives clues and sends him to inquire.
Even the teacher says: follow our good conduct, not the rest. Judgment stays with the student.

dilemmas.en: Betting a life on a lucky streak
dilemmas.desc: A sudden gain is taken as proof, and a large, hard-to-undo decision follows.
dilemmas.preyas: Wealth now, and the thrill of the streak.
dilemmas.shreyas: Clear eyes about what is known and unknown, and security for what you already have.

verses.why: The dull choose the pleasant 'for the sake of getting and keeping' (yoga-kṣema).
A person is not to be satisfied with wealth.
Enjoy by letting go; do not covet.
Naciketas refused the chain of wealth in which many sink.

dilemmas.en: Being told you are a genius
dilemmas.desc: The request asks for praise of an idea or a self, before testing it.
dilemmas.shreyas: An honest test of the idea before your savings are in it.

verses.why: 'If you think you know it well, you surely know very little.'
Śvetaketu came home conceited, thinking himself learned. His father's first question humbled him.
The gods took the victory for their own.
Examine the worlds won by works before committing yourself to them.

dilemmas.desc: Attention pulled outward by what is designed to hold it.
dilemmas.shreyas: Attention returned to what you actually care about.

verses.why: The senses were made outward-turning; so one looks outward and not within.
The childish run after outward desires into the wide net of death.
These pleasures last till tomorrow and wear out the vigour of the senses.
There is no joy in the small; the boundless is joy.

dilemmas.en: Wanting to hurt the one who hurt you
dilemmas.desc: The request asks for help to wound, expose or humiliate.
dilemmas.preyas: The satisfaction of a devastating reply.
dilemmas.shreyas: Restraint now, and a response you will still stand by later.

verses.why: Da: restrain yourselves.
Da: be compassionate.
As one's desire, so one's will; as one's will, so one's deed.
With discernment the mind is held steady and the senses obey.

dilemmas.en: Grief and the fear of ending
dilemmas.desc: The question of what remains when someone dies, or when one will.
dilemmas.shreyas: Facing the question Naciketas asked, at the pace grief allows.

verses.why: Naciketas asks the question every mourner asks: when a person dies, does something remain?
The knowing Self is not born and does not die.
If the slayer thinks he slays, or the slain thinks he is slain, neither understands.
'Lead me from death to immortality.'

dilemmas.desc: Learning accumulates, but the sorrow it was meant to address does not lift.
dilemmas.shreyas: Knowing what one's knowing is for.

verses.why: Nārada: 'I know only the texts, not the Self; and I am in sorrow.'
Not by discourse, not by intellect, not by much learning is the Self attained.
Even the Vedas are counted as the lower knowledge.
It is understood by those who do not claim to understand it.

dilemmas.en: Exhaustion and the right to rest
dilemmas.desc: Pushing on past depletion, and doubting whether rest is allowed.
dilemmas.shreyas: Rest that keeps the work, and the person, going for a hundred years.

verses.why: Doing one's work here, one should wish to live a hundred years: a long horizon, not a sprint.
From food are beings born and by food they live: the body is the first sheath of the self.
Deep, dreamless sleep is counted among the self's states, 'full of bliss'.

dilemmas.en: Living someone else's choice to keep the peace
dilemmas.desc: The request asks for permission to give up one's own path because family expects another, and to be told that doing so is right.
dilemmas.preyas: Agreement that ends the guilt today.
dilemmas.shreyas: Honour the parents and still hold one's own reins: decide with them, not merely for them.

verses.why: Treat mother and father as gods; and follow only the blameless deeds, not the others.
The good and the pleasant both approach a person; the wise one examines both and chooses.
The intellect is the charioteer: the reins are one's own.
As one's desire, so one's will; as one's will, so one's deed.

dilemmas.desc: The request asks for relief from comparison by a verdict: either 'you are behind' or 'it does not matter at all'.
dilemmas.preyas: A slogan that stops the feeling for an evening.
dilemmas.shreyas: Seeing that worth is not a rank, while still taking the work seriously.

verses.why: Joy is in the boundless; there is no joy in the small.
On the same tree the self, deluded and powerless, grieves; when it sees the other, the Lord, it is freed from sorrow.
For one who sees all beings as the Self, what delusion, what sorrow?
The pleasant and the good: the relief of a verdict, or the harder good of seeing clearly.

stories.title: Naciketas and Death
stories.summary: A boy given away to Death waits three nights at his door, is offered every pleasure in exchange for his question, and refuses them all.

stories.title: Indra and Virocana
stories.summary: Two students hear Prajāpati's first answer. Virocana leaves satisfied and teaches it to his people; Indra sees the flaw, returns three times, and is taught the truth after a hundred and one years.

stories.title: Satyakāma tells the truth
stories.summary: Asked his lineage, a boy repeats his mother's honest answer that she does not know it. The teacher accepts him because he did not swerve from the truth.

stories.title: Uddālaka teaches Śvetaketu: “that thou art”
stories.summary: Śvetaketu returns from twelve years of study, proud and unable to say what makes the unheard heard. His father teaches him with clay, honey, rivers, a tree, a banyan seed and salt dissolved in water, and nine times says: that thou art.

stories.title: Nārada knows the texts
stories.summary: Nārada lists every science he has mastered and admits he is still in sorrow: he knows the words, not the Self. Sanatkumāra leads him to the boundless.

stories.title: Maitreyī's question
stories.summary: Offered half of a household's wealth, Maitreyī asks the only question that matters: 'What should I do with that which will not make me immortal?'

stories.title: Bhṛgu learns by inquiry
stories.summary: Bhṛgu asks his father for Brahman. Varuṇa gives him clues and sends him to find out. Five times Bhṛgu returns with a deeper answer, until he reaches bliss.

stories.title: The gods and the Yakṣa
stories.summary: The gods take a victory for their own. A mysterious being sets a blade of grass before Agni and Vāyu, who cannot burn or move it. Umā tells Indra who it was.

stories.title: Sukeśa will not lie
stories.summary: Sukeśa tells his teacher Pippalāda how a prince once asked him about the person of sixteen parts, and how he answered plainly that he did not know, because one who speaks untruth withers to the root.

stories.title: Gārgī questions Yājñavalkya
stories.summary: At Janaka's great debate, Gārgī presses Yājñavalkya on what the worlds are woven upon until he warns her not to ask too far; she returns with two questions like arrows and is answered with the Imperishable.

stories.title: Janaka and the light of the person
stories.summary: King Janaka asks Yājñavalkya what light a person has: the sun, the moon, fire, speech; and when all are gone, the Self is the light.

stories.title: Six seekers before Pippalāda
stories.summary: Six students come to the sage Pippalāda with fuel in hand. He makes them live a year in austerity, then answers six questions: on creation, breath, its rising and setting, sleep, OM and the Person of sixteen parts.

stories.title: Śaunaka asks Aṅgiras
stories.summary: The great householder Śaunaka asks: what is that by knowing which all this is known? Aṅgiras answers with the two knowledges, the lower and the higher.

stories.title: Jānaśruti and Raikva the cart-man
stories.summary: A generous king overhears two swans praising a sage who sits under a cart scratching his itch. He offers cattle and gold; Raikva sends him away until he comes with real humility.

stories.title: Upakosala and the fires
stories.summary: A student tends his teacher's fires for twelve years and falls ill with longing; the fires themselves teach him that Brahman is breath, joy and space.

stories.title: Aśvapati and the universal self
stories.summary: Five learned householders and Uddālaka go to King Aśvapati, each worshipping a part of the self; he teaches them the self that is all of it.

stories.title: Pravāhaṇa and the five fires
stories.summary: Śvetaketu, proud of his learning, cannot answer King Pravāhaṇa's five questions about where beings go after death. His father comes humbly to learn the teaching of the five fires.

stories.title: Ajātaśatru and the proud Bālāki
stories.summary: Bālāki offers to teach the king Brahman and names twelve forms of it; each is refuted, and the king leads him to a sleeping man to show where the self goes in sleep.

stories.title: Citra questions Śvetaketu
stories.summary: King Citra asks the young priest where the worlds after death end; neither son nor father knows, and both come to learn from the king.

stories.title: Indra teaches Pratardana
stories.summary: The king Pratardana wins his way to Indra's world and asks for the boon most beneficial to humans; Indra teaches him that he is prāṇa, the conscious self.

stories.title: King Bṛhadratha in the forest
stories.summary: Weary of a body made of bones, skin and decay, King Bṛhadratha gives up his kingdom and stands a thousand years in austerity until the sage Śākāyanya teaches him the Self.

stories.title: The Self creates the worlds
stories.summary: In the beginning the Self alone was; it thought, let me create the worlds, then their guardians, then food; and finally it entered the person through the crown of the head.

stories.title: Uṣasti eats the elephant-keeper's beans
stories.summary: In a famine a starving priest eats an elephant-keeper's leftover beans but refuses his water: one bends a rule to live, not for comfort. He then questions the court priests on the gods they chant to.

stories.title: The thunder says Da, Da, Da
stories.summary: Gods, humans and demons ask Prajāpati for teaching; to each he says only 'Da'. The gods hear restrain, the humans give, the demons be compassionate, and the thunder repeats it still.

stories.title: Śāṇḍilya's meditation
stories.summary: All this is Brahman. The self within the heart is smaller than a grain of rice and greater than the earth: Śāṇḍilya's teaching on how to meditate on it.

stories.title: Yājñavalkya at Janaka's court
stories.summary: King Janaka offers a thousand cows to the most learned of the Brahmins. Yājñavalkya has them driven away before anyone answers; one by one the court's scholars question him, from Aśvala to Gārgī and Śākalya, and none prevails.

stories.title: The gods, the demons and the breath
stories.summary: The gods chant the Udgītha to overcome the demons; each sense chants and is pierced by evil, until the breath in the mouth chants and the demons shatter against it like clods against a rock.

stories.title: The dogs' Udgītha
stories.summary: A satire on ritual for gain: hungry dogs ask a white dog to chant the Udgītha for food, and parade like priests before the hymn: ‘Om, let us eat! Om, let us drink!’

stories.title: Three sages on the Udgītha
stories.summary: Three learned men ask one another what the chant rests on; each answer is taken one step further, from heaven to space, until King Pravāhaṇa names space as the final support.

vedas.label: Ṛgveda
vedas.essence: The Veda of praise: hymns to the powers of the cosmos. Its Upanishads ask what consciousness itself is.

vedas.label: Yajurveda
vedas.essence: The Veda of the sacrificial formulas (yajus), in two sections: the Śukla (‘white’), formulas kept apart from their explanation, and the Kṛṣṇa (‘black’), the two woven together. Its Upanishads turn the rite inward: the Self that is full, the chariot of the self, the five sheaths, the one God in all.

sections.label: Śukla
sections.note: Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā and the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa: formulas kept apart from their explanation.

sections.label: Kṛṣṇa
sections.note: Taittirīya, Kaṭha and Maitrāyaṇī schools: formulas and explanation woven together.

vedas.label: Sāmaveda
vedas.essence: The Veda of chant. Its Upanishads begin from the sung OM and end in ‘that thou art’.

vedas.label: Atharvaveda
vedas.essence: The Veda of everyday life and protection. Its Upanishads give the higher and lower knowledge, the six questions and the four states.

glossary.short: The good: what actually serves you over time, even when it is not what you want right now.
The pleasant: what gratifies now, such as praise, comfort or agreement; not evil, but binding when chosen for its own sake.
Discernment: telling the real from the apparent, and what you know from what you only hope.
The Self: what you most essentially are, the awareness that witnesses every thought and state.
The one Reality underlying everything that exists; the Upanishads teach that it is not other than the Self.
Breath, and the life-force behind every faculty; when it leaves the body, the senses go with it.
One of four 'great sayings' (such as 'that thou art') that state the identity of the Self and Brahman.
Essence: the Upanishads are called the sāra of the Vedas, the meaning their hymns and rites point to.
Literally 'sitting down near' a teacher: the philosophical closing teachings of each Veda.
A verse or formula of the Veda, meant to be heard and chanted as well as read.
The peace invocation chanted before and after a text, ending 'oṃ śāntiḥ śāntiḥ śāntiḥ'.
A commentary that explains a text word by word; here, almost always Śaṅkara's.
Ādi Śaṅkara (c. 8th century), whose commentaries read the Upanishads as teaching one Self without a second (Advaita).
'Not two': the reading of the Upanishads in which the Self and Brahman are one reality.
'The end of the Veda': the Upanishads, and the schools of thought built on them.
The collected hymns or formulas of a Veda, the oldest layer of the text.
The prose layer of a Veda that explains the rituals; several Upanishads close a Brāhmaṇa.
'Forest book': the layer of a Veda that turns the ritual into meditation, bridging Brāhmaṇa and Upanishad.
A 'branch': one school's recension of a Veda, with its own text of the hymns and teachings.
Freedom: release from the cycle of birth and death, reached by knowing the Self.
Action, and the way actions shape the doer and what comes next.
The round of births and deaths that continues as long as one acts from desire and ignorance.
Right conduct and the order it upholds; what is fitting to do.
The cosmic order the Vedas praise; truth spoken is its human form.
Truth, and the real; 'truth alone triumphs' is from the Muṇḍaka.
Disciplined effort, literally 'heat': the sustained inquiry by which Bhṛgu learned Brahman.
Trust: the confidence that makes one listen, act and keep inquiring.
Bliss: the joy that is the Self's own nature, not borrowed from objects.
The sacred syllable that stands for Brahman; its sounds map waking, dream, deep sleep and the silence beyond.
'The Fourth': pure awareness beyond waking, dream and deep sleep, present in all three.
A 'sheath' of the person: food, breath, mind, understanding and bliss, from outer to inner.
The power by which the one appears as many.
One of nature's three strands: clarity (sattva), passion (rajas) and inertia (tamas).
'The Person': the conscious principle, and in the Ṛgveda the cosmic being from whom all arose.
'Imperishable': Brahman as that which does not decay; also 'syllable', so OM.
The witness: the one who looks on, like the second bird that watches without eating.
Knowledge; the higher vidyā is knowing the Imperishable, the lower is learning about the world.
Ignorance: not a lack of facts but taking oneself to be what one is not.
'Yoking': the steady holding of the senses and mind, defined in the Kaṭha.
A qualified teacher; the Upanishads insist the Self is learned from one who has realized it.
One's own study: learning and recitation done by oneself, kept up for life.
The Lord: God as ruler within all things.
'Not this, not this': no description fits Brahman, so every description is set aside.
'That thou art': Uddālaka's teaching to his son that the subtle essence of all things is your own Self.
Grace: the Self reveals itself to the one it chooses, not to effort alone.
Charioteer: in the Kaṭha, the intellect that holds the reins of the mind; 'Upa-sārathi' is the charioteer who sits near.
The 'I-maker': the sense of a separate ego, inflated by flattery and by false certainty.
Compassion: truth delivered with care.
Desire: as one's desire, so one's will; as one's will, so one's deed.
A sense-power: in the Kaṭha's chariot, the horses that run toward their objects.
The intellect that discerns and decides: the charioteer of the Kaṭha.
The mind that perceives and wants: the reins of the chariot.
A standard way of writing Sanskrit in Latin letters, with marks for long vowels and special sounds (ā, ṛ, ś, ṣ, ṃ).
The script in which Sanskrit is usually written today.
A 'creeper': the name for a chapter in the Kaṭha and Taittirīya.
A lesson or section, the unit of recitation in the Taittirīya.
A section of a chapter.
A lesson or chapter, used in the Chāndogya and Maitrī.
Bādarāyaṇa's aphorisms that systematize the Upanishads' teaching; with the Upanishads and the Gītā, one of Vedānta's three sources.
'Knowledge': the four oldest scriptures of India (Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, Atharva), of which the Upanishads are the closing part.
